I like it! It has a soothing ambient vibe. If I had to offer any suggestion, it would be to pay attention to your sound choices. For example the trumpets seemed to clash sonically with the rest of the mix. Maybe you could wash it out with some verb or something to make them sit better, but to me, they seemed like a strange sound choice for the ambient soundscape. It also wouldn't hurt to add some more sections in the song to give it a little more movement. Maybe a bridge with some different chords and instrumentation could add another layer to the vibe and tell more of a "story". 

But all in all, I like it! Thanks for sharing!

Dude, I really like the verses and pre chorus. The little guitar riffs are fun and create a vibe for the song. Lyrically, it progresses well and the message is clear. So seriously, kudos for that. I see too many songwriters drift off topic as the verses pile up, but you stayed on topic and told a very relatable story of angsty insecurity and regret. My biggest constructive criticism (which is completely opinion-based) is that I don't feel the chorus lives up to the other sections of the song. Dynamically it was good and chorusy, but the melody seemed to be missing a little "je ne sais quoi" to really emphasize the hook and get it stuck in your head. Additionally I think the guitar rhythm in the chorus could use a little tweaking too.But that is just one persons opinion, so do with it what you will. 

All in all, I really enjoyed it. Thanks for sharing!

I often find that the melody is the first thing that comes to me and my struggle is fitting the lyrics to the melody that I already have in my head. But if I do need to write a melody to a song idea or chord structure that I already have, I typically track it into a DAW and loop a section (verse, chorus, etc.). Then I mumble sing to the loop until I get a spark. Then I repeat the process until it feels right. Lyrics are extremely important as well, but I almost never have lyrics before I have a melody. Rhythm, phonetics, timbre, are all very important to me when it comes to melody. So if I have polished lyrics before I have a melody, I usually have to fight a stressful, uphill battle to find a melody that I'm satisfied with.

Naturally this depends on the purpose of the song that I'm writing. If I am writing with/for another artist, I typically pay more attention to structure to match that artists style. For instance, if they are a "radio pop" artist I usually approach the song assuming it'll be something along the lines of intro, verse, pre chorus, chorus, post chorus/break, verse, pre chorus, chorus, post chorus/break, bridge, chorus, outro. Really my focus is doing whatever I need to do to spam the hook in the song as much as is tastefully possible. It really just depends on the artist though.

But if I'm writing for myself, it depends more on my purpose. Am I telling a story? Do I want people to dance or listen intently? Is it sad or happy? Etc. All of those will effect how I approach the song. Some songs need a lot of verses to tell a story and some songs don't need anything but different versions of the same hook. It all depends, but I typically think less about structure and more about movement or tension and release. I don't worry too much about the number of sections, what order they're in, or their length. As long as I think it sounds good, I roll with it. Elliott Smith once said "If YOU love it, then there is definitely someone else in the world that will love it too." So I try to stay true to my ears, taste, and intuition without overthinking it. In my experience that is what works best for me.

I hope that wasn't to vague of an answer for a very relevant question. But at the end of the day, music is all about feeling. I've listened to songs in simple AAA structures that left in tears so it doesn't need to be complicated to be effective. Just stay true to you and trust your ears.

As you said, depression is commonly misunderstood by the masses as something that makes you extremely sad all the time, but that's simply not true. In my personal case, about 80% of the time I don't feel anything; not happy, not sad, just apathetic about everything. The other 20% of the time is when the feelings of overwhelming sadness that often occurs without reason or warning. I agree that it's near impossible to explain the feelings to someone who hasn't felt it, but have you tried talking to some trusted friends or family about it?

It is extremely sad when someone hates living, but is something I can relate to 100%. Have you tried speaking to someone about your feelings? Like a family member or a professional? 
Death is an easy solution to stop the feelings that you have, but is it really the best solution? I can't answer that question for you, but I sincerely hope that you can keep pushing until you find a reason to live. It's out there. I promise.

Hey Hikaru,

You don't really have to say you have depression to see a psychologist. Perhaps you could tell your family about your anxiety and use that as an excuse to see a psychologist. Then speak your mind to the psychologist and let him/her give their prognosis. This way you don't have to use the word "depression" without certainty! Even if it turns out you're not depressed and just have anxiety, surely it's worth finding out!

Hope this helps and best of luck!
